newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean prosecutors begin grilling Hanbo officials.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean prosecutors begin grilling Hanbo officials.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors have begun questioning executives of the troubled Hanbo Group on how $5.8 billion of loans were funnelled to its foundering steelmaking unit, prosecution officials said on Wednesday.
They also sifted through Hanbo documents seized by police from offices of Hanbo Steel Co and its 15 affiliates on Tuesday.
"The investigation team started summoning Hanbo officials last night," one official said. "Three executives and other officials responsible for Hanbo's financial affairs have been questioned."

Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate, is awaiting a Seoul court decision on receivership that would protect it from creditors. The second largest steelmaker in South Korea defaulted on debt payments last week.
It piled up loans of five trillion won ($5.8 billion) from 61 banks and financial institutions, mainly to build a new steel mill in the southwestern town of Tangjin.
Another prosecution official said investigators would soon probe current and former heads of four main creditor banks to piece together information that could shed light on the loan scandal.
The Justice Ministry on Tuesday slapped overseas travel bans on Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank, Korea Exchange Bank and Korea Development Bank along with 13 others.
A total of 29 people, including Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo and his top aides, have been banned from leaving the country over the scandal.

President Kim Young-sam on Monday ordered a thorough probe into the loans after the opposition accused his government of pressuring creditors to keep providing loans despite the lack of adequate collateral.

With the opposition seizing on the Hanbo controversy to keep pressure on the government in an electon year, Kim on Tuesday indefinitely postponed a planned visit to Hungary, Poland, Turkey and Italy in early March.
Kim swept to power in 1993 on an anti-graft ticket but his drive against corruption is once again on the line ahead of presidential elections in December.
The president has promised to end legacies of the military- backed strongman rule of his predecessors by severing corrupt alliance betweeen politics and business.

Kim sent former presidents Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo to trial for taking huge sums from businessmen by rewarding them with soft loans and expensive projects. Chun is now serving a life sentence and Roh a 17-year jail term.

A spokesman for Korea First Bank, which has the largest exposure to Hanbo with loans totalling 1.08 trillion won, said he expected the Seoul court to grant receivership soon to stop Hanbo's failure from sending shock waves to the economy.

The state Small and Medium Business Administration said on Wednesday about 150 suppliers and subcontractors to Hanbo Steel had suffered from a financial squeeze due to a payment freeze by the steelmaker.
Some of them have defaulted on their own debt repayments, an administration official said without giving details.

The Finance and Economy Ministry said the government would continue to pump cash into the money market to avoid a credit crunch. It said on Wednesday a further 2.0-2.5 trillion won would be released early next month after the central bank injected 3.6 trillion won since Friday. ($=857.5 won)
